new_statements.quote: In Pichi, an H tone is the only consistent indicator of prominence. There are other phonetic features which may increase the prominence of a syllable or series of syllables and may be exploited for stylistic effect. [...] But the data does not reveal any systematic appearance of other phonetic features with prominent syllables other than an H tone. Word stress in the sense of an automatic, metrically conditioned culmination of phonetic features other than pitch alone, does not exist in Pichi. Nevertheless, there are two features which I refer to as 'stress'. Firstly, an extra-high tone may be exploited to signal focus or emphasis (cf. 4.3.2). Secondly, Pichi employs lexical stress; certain types of words with grammatical and pragmatic functions almost exclusively occur with a higher-than-usual pitch (cf. 4.3.3).

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Pichi has an empty rule field and there are no existing stress statements, so nothing to contradict. Yakpo supplies the substantive classification: a tone language with a mixed pitch accent/tone system, an explicit statement that metrical word stress does not exist, and the positional restriction of the lexical H to only/penultimate/final syllable. If the catalog treats Pichi as a stress language, this source says it is not one: prominence is pitch (H tone) only.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Pichi is described as a tone language with a mixed pitch accent/tone system (p. 30: 'Pichi is a tone language which exhibits a mixed prosodic system.. Around 95% of the words in my corpus are characterised by pitch accent. In accented words only one syllable bears a lexically specified H tone while other syllables remain toneless. The remaining 5% are fully tonal words'). Metrical word stress does not exist (p. 97). The single lexical H of accented words falls on the only, penultimate or final syllable (p. 81: 'The near-totality of accented words bear a single H tone over their only, penultimate or final syllable'; p. 83: 'Most roots in the corpus, namely 94,6 percent therefore carry an H tone over the only syllable, the penultimate syllable or the final syllable'). Table 4.2 (p. 82): H monosyllables 54.1%, H.X (penultimate) 23.3%, X.H (final) 14.0%, L monosyllables 2.5%; minor classes X.H.X, H.H, X.X.H, H.X.X, L.H.H, L.L total 6%. Placement within a polysyllable is lexical (penultimate vs final), not predictable by rule, though the author notes it is 'forecastable' in that it is confined to these positions. The H tone delineates the prosodic word 'in very much the same way as stress in stress-accent languages' (p. 60). What the author calls 'stress' is (a) speaker-controlled emphatic stress = extra-high tone on the H syllable for focus/emphasis (§4.3.2) and (b) 'lexical stress' = a lexically assigned extra-high pitch on certain function words (question words, demonstratives, negators no/nɔto, if, mek 'SBJV', degree modifiers) (§4.3.1, Table 4.5 p. 97; §4.3.3 pp. 101-103).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described; no secondary stress. Accented words carry exactly one H tone; all other syllables toneless (default low). Emphatic extra-high tone may spread rightward onto following toneless syllables to the word boundary (p. 98).
new_statements.exceptions: About 5% of roots are fully tonal words with every syllable specified H or L (e.g. nyɔní 'ant' H.H, Bàta L.L, apás 'after' H.H, okobó L.H.H), many of African origin; these escape tone spreading/deletion and boundary tones. L-toned monosyllabic function words (dè, gò, bìn, à, è, =àn, fɔ̀, nà) are tonal and unstressable (Table 4.5). Spanish-origin words: 'Spanish stress-accent is generally converted into a Pichi pitch accent' (p. 79), usually a penultimate H mirroring Spanish penultimate stress (p. 83). Ideophones have idiosyncratic tonal patterns (p. 82). Compounds and clitic groups bear a single H like simplex words (p. 60).
new_statements.identity_note: Yakpo 2009 describes Pichi (Fernando Po Creole English), the Krio offshoot spoken on Bioko, Equatorial Guinea, based on the author's own fieldwork corpus there; it compares the system with Krio, Nigerian Pidgin, Saramaccan and other Atlantic creoles but the stress/tone claims are about Pichi itself. Spanish code-mixed material is treated separately (Spanish stress converted to Pichi pitch accent).

tone_statements.citation: Yakpo, Kofi. 2021. Creole Prosodic Systems Are Areal, Not Simple. Frontiers in Psychology 12: 690593. doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2021.690593 (open access, CC-BY; PMC8579057).
tone_statements.quote: Pichi has an ‘equipollent’ ( Hyman, 2011a ) 2-tone system with a High (H) and a Low (L) tone. This means that /H/ and /L/ are both lexically specified and phonologically activated, and subjected to tonal rules and processes (see section 2.1.2). There is no acoustic evidence for stress. The Pichi prosodic lexicon is etymologically layered due to the mechanism of stress-to-tone mapping that converted English stress to tone (section 4.1). Most English-sourced words, which constitute the majority of the lexicon, feature an obligatory (at least one) and cumulative (at most one) H tone.
tone_statements.locator: sec. 2.1.1 'Tones, Tone Patterns, and Minimal Pairs' (under 2.1 'A Creole With Tone: Pichi'); online article, no printed pagination (Front. Psychol. 12:690593)

tone_statements.summary: 2 level tones H and L (equipollent), syllable TBU, no stress; lexical + grammatical tone; downdrift and downstep, plateauing, OCP.

tone_statements.quote: Pichi has two phonological tones, a level H and a level L tone. The language features numerous monosyllabic tonal minimal pairs, for example, dé /H/ 'locative-existential copula' vs. dè /L/ 'imperfective marker' ... Most English-derived words, which constitute the majority of lexemes, bear at least and not more than one H, and the position of the H tone largely coincides with primary stress placement in the cognate forms of English. ... Pichi also has a number of tonal processes, including rightward H-tone spreading, tone sandhi and deletion, and a tone-conditioned suppletive allomorphy. ... Pichi features utterance-level downstep [p. 10]

tone_statements.summary: Confirms the catalog's tonal / lexical-tone coding and the 'no word stress' status. Details: two level tonemes H and L, no contour tonemes (contours = lexical tone + polar floating tone on one TBU); tone-bearing unit = syllable (vowels and sonorants /n m l r/); lexical tone contrasts a small set of monosyllables (bay 'by' vs báy 'buy', de 'ipfv' vs dé 'day'), morphological tone in pronoun paradigm

tone_statements.citation: Yakpo, Kofi (2013). Pichi. In English-based and Dutch-based Languages. Oxford: Oxford University Press. pp. 194-205.
tone_statements.quote: Pichi is a tone language with two phonemic tones, a high (H) and a low (L) tone, as well as a default low tone over toneless syllables. Hence we find monosyllabic tonal minimal pairs like de [H] 'locative-existential copula' vs. dè [L] 'imperfective marker'. The language also shows the maximal number of possible tonal configurations over bisyllabic words of the same syntactic category: fiba [HL] 'fever', wàtá [LH] 'water', nyɔní [HH] 'ant' and bàta [LL] 'buttocks'. Grammatical tone is used for inflection and derivation as well (see §5). Pichi exhibits a mixed prosodic system, a typologically unusual feature that characterizes other Atlantic creoles too (see e.g. Berry 1970, Rountree 1972, Devonish 2002, Good 2004, Rivera Castillo & Faraclas 2005). Hence, around 95 per cent of the words in the corpus bear a single pitch accent (an H tone). The remaining 5 per cent are tonal words in which all syllables are lexically specified for H or L tones. Tonal words are not normally affected by tonal processes such as tone spreading or deletion, nor do they bear intonational boundary tones.

sources.quote: Pichi is a tone language. [...] I therefore treat the prosodic system of Pichi as a tonal system tout court. [...] Pichi has two distinctive tonemes, namely a High (H) and a Low (L) tone. The language employs lexical and morphological tone, and there is an unevenly distributed number of tone classes. [...] The tone-bearing unit in Pichi is the syllable. || About 95 per cent of roots contained in my lexical data-base carry a single H tone over their only, penultimate, or final syllable. Other syllables in these words are L-toned. || But there is no stress in Pichi in the sense of an automatic, metrically conditioned culmination of phonetic features as in intonation-only languages.

sources.citation: Yakpo, Kofi (2013). Pichi. In English-based and Dutch-based Languages. Oxford: Oxford University Press. pp. 194-205.

sources.quote: Pichi is a tone language with two phonemic tones, a high (H) and a low (L) tone, as well as a default low tone over toneless syllables. Hence we find monosyllabic tonal minimal pairs like de [H] 'locative-existential copula' vs. dè [L] 'imperfective marker'. The language also shows the maximal number of possible tonal configurations over bisyllabic words of the same syntactic category: fiba [HL] 'fever', wàtá [LH] 'water', nyɔní [HH] 'ant' and bàta [LL] 'buttocks'. Grammatical tone is used for inflection and derivation as well (see §5). Pichi exhibits a mixed prosodic system, a typologically unusual feature that characterizes other Atlantic creoles too (see e.g. Berry 1970, Rountree 1972, Devonish 2002, Good 2004, Rivera Castillo & Faraclas 2005). Hence, around 95 per cent of the words in the corpus bear a single pitch accent (an H tone). The remaining 5 per cent are tonal words in which all syllables are lexically specified for H or L tones. Tonal words are not normally affected by tonal processes such as tone spreading or deletion, nor do they bear intonational boundary tones.

sources.citation: Yakpo, Kofi. 2021. Creole Prosodic Systems Are Areal, Not Simple. Frontiers in Psychology 12: 690593. doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2021.690593 (open access, CC-BY; PMC8579057).
sources.quote: Pichi has an ‘equipollent’ ( Hyman, 2011a ) 2-tone system with a High (H) and a Low (L) tone. This means that /H/ and /L/ are both lexically specified and phonologically activated, and subjected to tonal rules and processes (see section 2.1.2). There is no acoustic evidence for stress. The Pichi prosodic lexicon is etymologically layered due to the mechanism of stress-to-tone mapping that converted English stress to tone (section 4.1). Most English-sourced words, which constitute the majority of the lexicon, feature an obligatory (at least one) and cumulative (at most one) H tone.

sources.quote: Krio ..., Cameroon Pidgin ..., Nigerian Pidgin ..., Ghanaian Pidgin English ..., and Pichi have been analysed as languages that make use of lexical and grammatical tone (for a detailed acoustic and phonological analysis of the Pichi prosodic system, see Yakpo 2019: 37–73). ... H-toned syllables bear an acute accent, e.g. wét ‘wait’, and L-toned syllables a grave accent e.g. wèt ‘with’. ... The tonal specification of the two pronouns cannot be altered by pragmatic uses of pitch, e.g. for contrastive focus, as is common in intonation-only languages like Spanish and English.
